### Statistical analyses

Participant’s characteristics and self-reported questionnaires were analyzed with χ2 and independent t-tests, respectively. The Motor Sequencing App automatically uploaded the data to a cloud-based database. This task enabled us to compare patients with OCD and HV in the following measures: training engagement (which included as primary output measures of the total number of practices completed and app engagement as defined as the number of sequences attempted, including both correct and incorrect sequences); procedural learning, automaticity development, sensitivity to reward (see definitions and description of data analyses in Results section); and training effects on symptomatology as measured by the YBOCS difference pre-post training. The Phase B experiments enabled further investigation of preference and re-evaluation strategies. The primary outcome was the number of choices.

Between-group analyses were conducted using Kruskal-Wallis H tests when the normality assumption was violated. Parametric factorial analyses were carried out with ANOVA. Our alpha level of significance was 0.05. On the descriptive statistics, main values are represented as median, and errors are reported as interquartile range unless otherwise stated, due to the non-Gaussian distribution of the datasets. When conducting several tests related to the same hypothesis, or when running several post-hoc tests following factorial effects, we controlled the FDR at level p = 0.05. Significant values after FDR control are denoted by pFDR. Analyses were performed using Python version 3.7.6 and JASP version 0.14.1.0.

In the case of non-significant effects in the factorial analyses, we assessed the evidence in favor or against the full factorial model relative to the reduced model with BF (ratio BFfull/BFrestricted) using the bayesFactor toolbox (https://github.com/klabhub/bayesFactor, copy archived at Klabhu, 2020) in MATLAB. This toolbox implements tests that are based on multivariate generalizations of Cauchy priors on standardized effects (Rouder et al., 2012). As recommended by Rouder et al., 2012, we defined the restricted models as the full factorial model without one specific main or interaction effect. The ratio BFfull/BFrestricted represents the ratio between the probability of the data being observed under the full model and the probability of the same data under the restricted model. BF values were interpreted following Andraszewicz et al., 2015. The relationship between primary outcomes and clinical measures was calculated using a Pearson correlation.

The diurnal patterns of app use (Figure 2b and c) were assessed in each group using circular statistics (Mardia, 1975), with the ‘circular’ package in R (R version 4.3.1; 2023-06-16). This provided the group-level mean vector length and direction. To assess on the group level whether the daily practice data were uniformly distributed or, alternatively, oriented toward a specific time, we used a Rayleigh test (Landler et al., 2021; Mardia, 1975). We adapted code from Galvez-Pol et al., 2022. To test differences between two circular distributions (OCD, HV), we followed the recommendations of Landler et al., 2021, and employed the high-powered Watson’s U2 test, a non-parametric rank-based test (function watson.two.test in R).

## Review text

DOI: [10.7554/eLife.87346.4.sa1](https://doi.org/10.7554/eLife.87346.4.sa1)

It is known that aberrant habit formation is a characteristic of obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD). Habits can be defined according to the following features (Balleine and Dezfouli, 2019): rapid execution, invariant response topography, action 'chunking' and resistance to devaluation.

The extent to which OCD behavior is derived from enhanced habit formation relative to deficits in goal-directed behavior is a topic of debate in the current literature. This study examined habit-learning specifically (cf. deficits in goal-directed behavior) by regularly presenting, via smartphone, sequential learning tasks to patients with OCD and healthy controls. Participants engaged in the tasks every day over the course of a month. Automaticity, including the extent to which individual actions in the sequence become part of a unified 'chunk', was an important outcome variable. Following the 30 days of training, in-laboratory tasks were then administered to examine (1) if performing the learned sequences themselves had become rewarding (2) differences in goal-directed vs. habitual behavior.

Several hypotheses were tested, including:

Patients would have impaired procedural learning vs. healthy volunteers (this was not supported, possibly because there were fewer demands on memory in the task used here)

Once the task had been learned, patients would display automaticity faster (unexpectedly, patients were slower to display automaticity)

Habits would form faster under a continuous (vs. variable) reinforcement schedule

Exploratory analyses were also conducted: an interesting finding was that OCD patients with higher self-reported symptoms voluntarily completed more sessions with the habit-training app and reported a reduction in symptoms.

Strengths

This paper is well situated theoretically within the habit learning/OCD literature.

Daily training in a motor-learning task, delivered via smartphone, was innovative, ecologically valid and more likely to assay habitual behaviors specifically. Daily training is also more similar to studies with non-humans, making a better link with that literature. The use of a sequential-learning task (cf. tasks that require a single response) is also more ecologically valid.

The in-laboratory tests (after the 1 month of training) allowed the researchers to test if the OCD group preferred familiar, but more difficult, sequences over newer, simpler sequences.

Weaknesses

The authors were not able to test one criterion of habits, namely resistance to devaluation, due to the nature of the task.

The sample size was relatively small. Some potentially interesting individual differences within the OCD group could have been examined more thoroughly with a bigger sample (e.g., preference for familiar sequences). A larger sample may have allowed the statistical testing of any effects due to medication status.

The authors achieved their aims in that two groups of participants (patients with OCD and controls) engaged with the task over the course of 30 days. The repeated nature of the task meant that 'overtraining' was almost certainly established, and automaticity was demonstrated. This allowed the authors to test their hypotheses about habit learning. The results are supportive of the author's conclusions.

This article is likely to be impactful -- the delivery of a task across 30 days to a patient group is innovative and represents a new approach for the study of habit learning that is superior to an in-laboratory approach.

An interesting aspect of this manuscript is that it prompts a comparison with previous studies of goal-directed/habitual responding in OCD that used devaluation protocols, and which may have had their effects due to deficits in goal-directed behavior and not enhanced habit learning per se.

claims.claim: Dysfunctional goal-directed control in OCD has been strongly supported both behaviorally and from a neurobiological perspective.
claims.source: Dysfunctional goal-directed control in OCD has been strongly supported both behaviorally (Gillan et al., 2011; Vaghi et al., 2019) and from a neurobiological perspective (Gillan et al., 2015a).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous research (Gillan et al., 2011; Vaghi et al., 2019; Gillan et al., 2015a) demonstrating dysfunctional goal-directed control in OCD.

claims.claim: Enhanced habit formation in OCD has largely been inferred by the absence of goal-directed control.
claims.source: However, until now, enhanced (and potentially maladaptive) habit formation has largely been inferred by the absence of goal-directed control, although recent studies show increased self-reported habitual tendencies in OCD, as measured by the Self-Report Habit Index Scale (Ferreira et al., 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous research (Ferreira et al., 2017) and discussion of how habit formation has been inferred in the field.

claims.claim: Recent findings link stimulus-response strength and goal devaluation exclusively to a dysfunctional goal system.
claims.source: Problems with this 'zero-sum' hypothesis (Robbins and Costa, 2017) (i.e. diminished goal-directed control thus enhanced habitual control) have been reiterated by recent findings linking stimulus-response strength (Zwosta et al., 2018) and goal devaluation (Gillan et al., 2015b) exclusively to a dysfunctional goal system.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous research (Robbins and Costa, 2017; Zwosta et al., 2018; Gillan et al., 2015b) discussing problems with the zero-sum hypothesis.

claims.claim: Extensive training of sequential actions could be a means for rapidly engaging the 'habit system' in a laboratory setting.
claims.source: We recently proposed that extensive training of sequential actions could be a means for rapidly engaging the 'habit system' in a laboratory setting (Robbins et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous research (Robbins et al., 2019) proposing this methodological approach.

claims.claim: In action sequences, extensive training helps integrate separate motor actions into a coordinated and unified sequence, or 'chunk'.
claims.source: The idea is that, in action sequences (like those seen in skilled routines), extensive training helps integrate separate motor actions into a coordinated and unified sequence, or 'chunk' (Graybiel, 1998; Sakai et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous research (Graybiel, 1998; Sakai et al., 2003) on action sequence chunking.

claims.claim: For highly trained sequences, actions are represented in parallel according to their serial order before execution.
claims.source: Moreover, there is now robust evidence that for highly trained sequences, actions are represented in parallel according to their serial order before execution (Kornysheva et al., 2019).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous research (Kornysheva et al., 2019) on parallel representation of actions in trained sequences.

claims.claim: Automaticity is associated with a shift in control from the anterior/associative (goal-directed) to the posterior/sensorimotor (habitual) striatal regions.
claims.source: At a neural level, automaticity is associated with a shift in control from the anterior/associative (goal-directed) to the posterior/sensorimotor (habitual) striatal regions (Ashby et al., 2010; Graybiel and Grafton, 2015; Kupferschmidt et al., 2017), accompanied by a disengagement of cognitive control hubs in frontal and cingulate cortices (Bassett et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous research (Ashby et al., 2010; Graybiel and Grafton, 2015; Kupferschmidt et al., 2017; Bassett et al., 2015) on neural correlates of automaticity.

claims.claim: Within the skill learning literature, the progressive shift to posterior striatum has been linked to the gradually attained asymptotic performance of the skill.
claims.source: In fact, within the skill learning literature, this progressive shift to posterior striatum has been linked to the gradually attained asymptotic performance of the skill (Bassett et al., 2015; Doyon et al., 2018; Doyon et al., 2015; Lehéricy et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous research (Bassett et al., 2015; Doyon et al., 2018; Doyon et al., 2015; Lehéricy et al., 2005) on skill learning and striatal shifts.

claims.claim: Chunked action sequences provide an opportunity to target the brain's goal-habit transition and study the relationships between automaticity, skills, and habits.
claims.source: Hence, chunked action sequences provide an opportunity to target the brain's goal-habit transition and study the relationships between automaticity, skills, and habits (Dezfouli et al., 2014; Graybiel and Grafton, 2015; Robbins and Costa, 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous research (Dezfouli et al., 2014; Graybiel and Grafton, 2015; Robbins and Costa, 2017) on using chunked sequences to study habit formation.

claims.claim: Compulsions in OCD are often performed in a 'just right' manner, akin to skill learning.
claims.source: This approach is relevant for OCD research as it mimics the sequences of motor events and routines observed in typical compulsions, often performed in a ''just right'' manner (Hellriegel et al., 2017), akin to skill learning.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous research (Hellriegel et al., 2017) on the 'just right' nature of compulsions in OCD.

claims.claim: The Motor Sequencing App satisfies central criteria that define habits: swift execution, invariant response topography, and action chunking.
claims.source: This task, akin to a piano-based app, allows subjects to learn and practice two sequences of finger movements. It was tailored to emphasize the positive aspects of habits, as advocated by Watson et al., 2022, and it satisfies central criteria that define habits proposed by Balleine and Dezfouli, 2019: swift execution, invariant response topography, and action chunking.
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous research (Watson et al., 2022; Balleine and Dezfouli, 2019) defining criteria for habits.

claims.claim: The autonomous nature of habits and the fluid proficiency of skills engage the same sensorimotor cortical-striatal 'loops' (the so-called 'habit circuitry').
claims.source: Although there is no consensus on how exactly skills and habits interact (Robbins and Costa, 2017), it is generally agreed that both lead to automaticity with sufficient practice (Graybiel and Grafton, 2015) and that the autonomous nature of habits and the fluid proficiency of skills engage the same sensorimotor cortical-striatal 'loops' (the so-called 'habit circuitry') (Ashby et al., 2010; Graybiel and Grafton, 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous research (Robbins and Costa, 2017; Graybiel and Grafton, 2015; Ashby et al., 2010) on the relationship between habits, skills, and neural circuitry.

claims.claim: Outcome devaluation insensitivity as a test of habit in humans is controversial and may be a more sensitive indicator of failures of goal-directed control rather than of habitual control per se.
claims.source: This is important because outcome devaluation insensitivity as a test of habit in humans is controversial (Watson et al., 2022) and may indeed be a more sensitive indicator of failures of goal-directed control rather than of habitual control per se (Balleine and Dezfouli, 2019; Robbins et al., 2019; Robbins and Costa, 2017).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous research (Watson et al., 2022; Balleine and Dezfouli, 2019; Robbins et al., 2019; Robbins and Costa, 2017) discussing controversies around devaluation tests.

claims.claim: Training frequency, context stability, and reward contingencies are important features for enhancing habit strength.
claims.source: While designing our app, we additionally considered previous research emphasizing training frequency, context stability, and reward contingencies as important features for enhancing habit strength (Wood and Rünger, 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous research (Wood and Rünger, 2016) on factors enhancing habit strength.

claims.claim: Practice alone is insufficient for habit development as it also requires off-line consolidation over longer periods of time and sleep.
claims.source: To ensure effective consolidation required for habit/skill retention to occur, we implemented a 1-month training period. This aligns with studies showing that practice alone is insufficient for habit development as it also requires off-line consolidation over longer periods of time and sleep (Nusbaum et al., 2018; Walker et al., 2003).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to previous research (Nusbaum et al., 2018; Walker et al., 2003) on the role of consolidation and sleep in habit development.

claims.claim: Reinforcer predictability influences habit acquisition speed.
claims.source: Finally, given the influence of reinforcer predictability on habit acquisition speed (Bouton, 2021), we employed two different reinforcement schedules (reward scores: continuous versus variable [probabilistic]) to assess their impact on habit formation among healthy volunteers (HV) and patients with OCD.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to previous research (Bouton, 2021) on the influence of reinforcer predictability on habit acquisition.

claims.source: Anticipating implicit learning issues in OCD (Deckersbach et al., 2002; Kathmann et al., 2005; Rauch et al., 1997) and fine-motor difficulties (Bloch et al., 2011), we expected poorer procedural learning in patients compared to HV.

results.result: The study recruited 33 OCD patients and 34 healthy volunteers matched for age, gender, IQ, and years of education. After excluding two participants who did not meet minimum training requirements, the final sample consisted of 32 OCD patients (19 females) and 33 healthy volunteers (19 females), with most participants being right-handed.
results.evaluation: Claims C92-C95 provide clear descriptive statistics about participant recruitment, exclusions, and final sample composition. These are straightforward methodological details that are internally consistent and appropriately documented.

results.result: Healthy volunteers practiced the motor sequencing app preferentially at approximately 15:00, while OCD patients practiced at approximately 18:00, though there were no significant differences in daily training patterns between groups.
results.evaluation: Claims C3-C5 are supported by appropriate circular statistics (Rayleigh test for within-group patterns, Watson's U2 test for between-group comparison). The statistical tests are appropriate for circular data, and the non-significant between-group difference (p = 0.19) is properly reported despite the different peak times.

results.result: OCD patients do not exhibit learning deficits in motor sequence acquisition, achieving similar asymptotic performance as healthy volunteers despite initially slower performance. However, OCD patients took significantly longer to achieve automaticity and exhibited more variability in their progression.
results.evaluation: Claims C9 and C14 are supported by exponential decay modeling showing similar learning rates and asymptotic performance between groups, but significant differences in automaticity parameters (nC and CL). The statistical analyses appropriately distinguish between learning (MT parameters) and automaticity (C parameters), with Bayesian analyses supporting null effects where appropriate.

results.result: Both OCD patients and healthy volunteers speeded up sequence performance more following reward decrements than increments, with this sensitivity attenuating from the first to second practice bin. Both groups showed comparable overall changes in movement time during training, though the relative improvement depended on whether reward increased or decreased.
results.evaluation: Claims C15-C20 are supported by appropriate three-way ANOVA analyses with significant main effects and interactions properly reported. Post-hoc tests with FDR correction are appropriately applied. Bayesian analysis (BF = 6.08) provides moderate evidence for the absence of group effects on overall MT changes, which is properly interpreted.

results.result: The variability of trial-to-trial movement time changes was greater in OCD patients than healthy volunteers. Over training, both groups exhibited less variable changes in response to reward, with reward decrements associated with more variable behavioral changes than increments.
results.evaluation: Claims C21-C23 are supported by three-way ANOVA on standard deviation measures showing significant main effects of group (p = 9.93 × 10⁻⁶), bin (p = 2 × 10⁻¹⁶), and reward (p = 4.13 × 10⁻⁵). The statistical approach of analyzing distribution spread is appropriate for assessing behavioral variability.

results.result: Both groups exhibited increased IKI consistency over training, but OCD patients had less consistent timing patterns trial-to-trial compared to healthy volunteers. IKI consistency improved more following reward increments than decrements, with the variability of consistency values decreasing across practice bins.
results.evaluation: Claims C24-C27 are supported by three-way ANOVA analyses showing significant main effects of bin (p = 0.00607), group (p = 0.00454), and reward (p = 1.86 × 10⁻⁶) on IKI consistency measures. The analyses appropriately examine both central tendency and spread of distributions, with Bayesian analyses supporting null interaction effects.

results.result: When given the option to play an easier-but-shorter sequence, both groups significantly preferred it over the trained app sequence. However, participants with greater habitual tendencies showed greater propensity to prefer the trained app sequence.
results.evaluation: Claims C28-C29 are supported by Kruskal-Wallis test showing significant condition effect (H = 23.2, p < 0.001) and Pearson correlation (r = 0.36, p = 0.005) between COHS scores and app sequence preference. Post-hoc tests with FDR correction appropriately identify which conditions differ.

results.result: OCD patients with improved symptomatology after app training showed significantly greater preference for the trained app sequence compared to patients with unchanged or worsened symptoms. Greater symptom improvement correlated with greater preference for the familiar sequence, particularly when choosing between the trained sequence and a 3-move alternative.
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C31 are based on exploratory post-hoc subgroup analyses not pre-specified in the study design. While the statistical tests show significant effects (pFDR = 0.015, 0.011; rs = 0.35, p = 0.04), the subgroup analysis involves multiple comparisons and small sample sizes (14 improved vs 18 stable/worse), raising concerns about statistical power and potential Type I error inflation despite FDR correction.

results.result: Both groups were highly sensitive to re-evaluation based on monetary feedback, choosing the non-app sequence more often. However, when re-evaluation required motor effort, OCD patients significantly favored the trained app sequence over healthy volunteers.
results.evaluation: Claims C32-C33 are supported by appropriate statistical tests showing no group effect for monetary conditions (p = 0.210, BF = 0.742) but significant group × condition 4 interaction (p = 0.04) for the effort condition. The Bayesian analysis appropriately supports the null effect for monetary re-evaluation.

results.result: Symptom improvement in OCD patients was positively correlated with habitual tendencies (particularly routine subscale), with patients showing greater improvement having more pronounced habit routines. Patients who considered the app beneficial had higher compulsivity scores and habitual tendencies.
results.evaluation: Claims C36-C38 are based on exploratory analyses with strong correlations (r = 0.45, 0.80, 0.77) but involve post-hoc subgrouping and multiple comparisons. The three-way ANOVA (F = 13.7, p < 0.001) comparing symptom change subgroups is not clearly described in terms of the other factors. These exploratory findings require replication in a pre-registered study with adequate power.

results.result: In healthy volunteers, greater tendency for automatic behaviors correlated with finding the app more relaxing, but this correlation was not observed in OCD patients. Patients' symptom improvement did not correlate with how relaxing they found the app or the number of practices performed.
results.evaluation: Claims C39-C41 are supported by appropriate Pearson correlation analyses showing significant correlation in HV (r = 0.44, p < 0.01) but not in OCD (p = 0.1), and non-significant correlations between symptom improvement and relaxation (p = 0.1) or practice number (p = 0.2). The differential pattern between groups is appropriately documented.

results.result: OCD patients reported significantly higher intolerance of uncertainty, elevated motivation to avoid aversive outcomes, higher perfectionism, higher worries, and higher perceived stress compared to healthy controls.
results.evaluation: Claims C42-C46 are supported by independent t-tests showing significant group differences on multiple self-report questionnaires (IUS, BIS, FMPS, PSWQ, PSS), with reference to Table 1 and Figure 10. These are standard clinical characterization measures appropriately analyzed with parametric tests.

results.result: The goal/habit imbalance theory of compulsion in OCD postulates enhanced habit formation and impaired goal/habit arbitration. While dysfunctional goal-directed control has been strongly supported, enhanced habit formation has largely been inferred from the absence of goal-directed control, with recent findings linking stimulus-response strength and goal devaluation exclusively to dysfunctional goal systems.
results.evaluation: Claims C47-C50 accurately represent the theoretical framework and prior literature, supported by appropriate citations (Gillan et al., 2011, 2015a, 2015b; Vaghi et al., 2019; Zwosta et al., 2018; Robbins and Costa, 2017; Ferreira et al., 2017). These claims establish the theoretical context for the current study.

results.result: Extensive training of sequential actions can rapidly engage the habit system by integrating separate motor actions into coordinated chunks. Automaticity is associated with neural shifts from anterior/associative to posterior/sensorimotor striatal regions, and chunked action sequences provide an opportunity to study goal-habit transitions relevant to OCD compulsions.
results.evaluation: Claims C51-C57 accurately represent established neuroscience literature on motor sequence learning, habit formation, and neural correlates of automaticity, supported by appropriate citations (Robbins et al., 2019; Graybiel, 1998; Sakai et al., 2003; Kornysheva et al., 2019; Ashby et al., 2010; Graybiel and Grafton, 2015; Bassett et al., 2015; Hellriegel et al., 2017). These claims establish the scientific rationale for the methodological approach.

results.result: The Motor Sequencing App was designed to satisfy central criteria for habits (swift execution, invariant topography, action chunking) and incorporated features known to enhance habit strength (training frequency, context stability, reward contingencies, extended training period, reinforcer predictability). The approach avoids reliance on controversial outcome devaluation tests.
results.evaluation: Claims C58-C63 accurately describe the methodological design rationale, supported by appropriate citations to habit formation literature (Watson et al., 2022; Balleine and Dezfouli, 2019; Robbins and Costa, 2017; Wood and Rünger, 2016; Nusbaum et al., 2018; Walker et al., 2003; Bouton, 2021). The design choices are well-justified based on prior research.

results.result: Based on prior literature reporting implicit learning issues, fine-motor difficulties, and heightened sensitivity to negative feedback in OCD, the authors expected poorer procedural learning in patients compared to healthy volunteers.
results.evaluation: Claims C64-C66 accurately represent prior literature establishing the study hypotheses, supported by appropriate citations (Deckersbach et al., 2002; Kathmann et al., 2005; Rauch et al., 1997; Bloch et al., 2011; Apergis-Schoute et al., 2024; Becker et al., 2014; Kanen et al., 2019). These claims establish the a priori expectations.

results.result: The study successfully achieved automaticity, fulfilling three of four criteria for habits (rapid execution, invariant topography, chunked sequences) but was unable to test resistance to devaluation. The app-trained sequences likely encompass both habitual and goal-directed qualities, aligning with contemporary perspectives on skilled/habitual sequences.
results.evaluation: Claims C72-C75 provide an honest assessment of what the study achieved and its limitations. The acknowledgment of the inability to test devaluation (C73) is appropriate, and the interpretation that sequences have mixed properties (C75) is supported by citation to contemporary theory (Du and Haith, 2023). This represents appropriate scientific caution in interpretation.

results.result: The tendency to attribute higher intrinsic value to familiar actions may be a potential mechanism leading to compulsions and represents an important addition to the goal/habit imbalance hypothesis. Smartphone app training has potential as a habit reversal therapeutic tool.
results.evaluation: Claims C67-C69 represent speculative interpretations and conclusions that extend beyond the data. While the preference findings (C28-C33) and exploratory symptom improvement analyses (C30-C31, C36-C38) provide some support, these are exploratory findings requiring replication. The therapeutic potential (C68) is particularly speculative given the lack of a controlled clinical trial design.

results.result: The authors propose that behavior may be generally goal-directed but vary in the balance of control by external versus internal goals, and that the dual process framework might be better understood in terms of extrinsic versus intrinsic outcomes. Habits may acquire alternative sources of value rather than losing current value.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C78 represent theoretical speculation and reinterpretation of the dual process framework based on the study findings. While supported by citations to theoretical work (Hommel and Wiers, 2017; Kruglanski and Szumowska, 2020; O'Doherty, 2014), these are speculative proposals that require further empirical testing and are not directly demonstrated by the current data.

results.result: The finding of no procedural learning deficits in OCD is inconsistent with prior SRT paradigm studies but aligns with recent studies showing successful learning with explicit instructions. The current task may tap less into memory processes than SRT tasks because sequences were explicitly demonstrated before training.
results.evaluation: Claims C79-C81 appropriately contextualize the current findings relative to prior literature, with appropriate citations (Deckersbach et al., 2002; Joel et al., 2005; Kathmann et al., 2005; Rauch et al., 2001, 1997; Soref et al., 2018; Barzilay et al., 2022). The inference about task differences (C81) is reasonable and helps explain the discrepancy with prior findings.

results.result: While heightened sensitivity to negative feedback in motor learning has been documented in the general population, the current findings do not support differences between OCD and healthy individuals in sensitivity to negative score changes, unlike previous work highlighting increased response switching after negative feedback in OCD.
results.evaluation: Claims C82-C83 appropriately contextualize the current null findings relative to prior literature, with appropriate citations (Abe et al., 2011; Galea et al., 2015; Pekny et al., 2015; van Mastrigt et al., 2020; Hauser et al., 2017; Marzuki et al., 2021). The discussion of potential reasons for the discrepancy (implicit vs explicit feedback, training duration) is reasonable.

results.result: Previous studies have reported that subjective habitual tendencies are associated with compulsive traits and act as predictors of subclinical OCD symptomatology in healthy populations.
results.evaluation: Claim C84 accurately represents prior literature, supported by appropriate citations (Ersche et al., 2019; Wuensch et al., 2022; Ramakrishnan et al., 2022). This provides context for interpreting the self-report findings in the current study.

results.result: The habit replacement hypothesis suggests that trained action sequences may disrupt OCD compulsions by engaging the same neural habit circuitry, in line with successful interventions in Tourette syndrome, tic disorders, and trichotillomania.
results.evaluation: Claims C85 and C71 represent speculative hypotheses about therapeutic mechanisms, supported by citations to related disorders (Hwang et al., 2012; Bate et al., 2011; Morris et al., 2013). However, the current study does not directly test this mechanism, and the exploratory symptom improvement findings are insufficient to support this specific mechanistic interpretation.

results.result: The study was unable to employ resistance to devaluation as a criterion because it would have invalidated subsequent tests. The utility of the devaluation criterion has been questioned in human habit learning studies, and recent analyses have not employed devaluation as a criterion.
results.evaluation: Claims C86-C88 provide appropriate acknowledgment of methodological limitations and contextualize these within ongoing debates in the field, supported by citation to recent work (Du and Haith, 2023). This represents appropriate scientific transparency about study limitations.

results.result: The monetary discounting condition involved deterministic choice with non-overlapping reward ranges, while the effort discounting condition had equivalent reward ranges creating uncertainty. The probabilistic constraint in the effort condition may account for greater task sensitivity in OCD given patients' susceptibility to uncertainty.
results.evaluation: Claims C89-C91 provide reasonable post-hoc interpretation of why the effort condition showed group differences while monetary conditions did not, supported by citation to literature on uncertainty in OCD (Pushkarskaya et al., 2015). This is appropriate scientific reasoning about task design effects.

results.result: Both healthy volunteers and OCD patients showed preferred practice times (HV at ~15:00, OCD at ~18:00), but there were no significant differences in daily training patterns between groups.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not raise concerns about these descriptive findings regarding practice timing patterns. The editor noted that 'participants engaged in the tasks every day over the course of a month,' implicitly accepting the reported practice patterns.

results.result: OCD patients did not exhibit learning deficits in motor sequence acquisition, contrary to previous implicit learning studies using serial reaction time paradigms. This finding aligns with recent studies showing successful learning in OCD when instructions are given explicitly.
results.evaluation: The reviewer explicitly noted that 'Patients would have impaired procedural learning vs. healthy volunteers (this was not supported, possibly because there were fewer demands on memory in the task used here),' accepting the finding while acknowledging the methodological explanation provided by the authors.

results.result: OCD patients took significantly longer to achieve a similar level of automaticity in both reward schedules compared to healthy volunteers, beginning at a slower pace with more variability.
results.evaluation: The reviewer explicitly stated that 'Once the task had been learned, patients would display automaticity faster (unexpectedly, patients were slower to display automaticity),' acknowledging this finding as contrary to the hypothesis but accepting it as a valid result.

results.result: Both OCD and healthy volunteer participants showed comparable sensitivity to reward feedback, speeding up more following score drops than increases, with improvements over practice. No group differences were found in overall movement time changes during training.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these findings on reward sensitivity. The results are consistent with the reviewer's acknowledgment that the study successfully examined habit learning through repeated training, and no concerns were raised about the reward feedback analyses.

results.result: OCD patients showed greater variability in trial-to-trial movement time changes compared to healthy volunteers, though both groups exhibited reduced variability over training. Reward decrements were associated with more variable behavioral changes than increments.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not question these findings on movement time variability. The results support the overall conclusion that 'patients were slower to display automaticity,' which the reviewer explicitly acknowledged.

results.result: Both groups showed increased consistency of inter-keystroke interval patterns over training, but OCD patients had less consistent timing patterns trial-to-trial compared to healthy volunteers. IKI consistency improved more following reward increments than decrements.
results.evaluation: The reviewer noted that 'Automaticity, including the extent to which individual actions in the sequence become part of a unified 'chunk', was an important outcome variable' and that 'automaticity was demonstrated,' accepting these findings as evidence of chunking and automaticity differences between groups.

results.result: When given easier alternatives, both groups preferred them over the trained app sequence. However, participants with greater habitual tendencies showed greater preference for the trained sequence. OCD patients with symptom improvement showed significantly greater preference for the trained sequence.
results.evaluation: The reviewer explicitly noted that 'The in-laboratory tests (after the 1 month of training) allowed the researchers to test if the OCD group preferred familiar, but more difficult, sequences over newer, simpler sequences' as a strength, accepting these preference findings as valid results.

results.result: Both groups were highly sensitive to monetary re-evaluation, choosing higher-reward sequences regardless of novelty. However, when re-evaluation required motor effort, OCD patients significantly favored the trained app sequence over healthy volunteers.
results.evaluation: The reviewer acknowledged the study examined 'differences in goal-directed vs. habitual behavior' through in-laboratory tests. The finding that OCD patients favored familiar sequences under effort conditions aligns with the reviewer's statement that results are 'supportive of the author's conclusions.'

results.result: Symptom improvement in OCD patients correlated positively with habitual tendencies (particularly routine subscale) and with subjective ratings of app benefit. Patients with higher compulsivity and habitual tendencies considered the app more beneficial. In healthy volunteers, automaticity tendencies correlated with finding the app relaxing.
results.evaluation: The reviewer explicitly noted as an 'interesting finding' that 'OCD patients with higher self-reported symptoms voluntarily completed more sessions with the habit-training app and reported a reduction in symptoms,' accepting these exploratory correlational findings.

results.result: OCD patients reported significantly higher intolerance of uncertainty, elevated motivation to avoid aversive outcomes, and higher perfectionism, worries, and perceived stress compared to healthy controls.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge these standard clinical characterization findings. These results are consistent with established OCD profiles and serve to characterize the patient sample appropriately.

results.result: The study successfully achieved automaticity, fulfilling three of four criteria for habits (rapid execution, invariant topography, chunked sequences) but was unable to test resistance to devaluation. The trained sequences likely encompass both habitual and goal-directed qualities.
results.evaluation: The reviewer explicitly identified as a weakness that 'The authors were not able to test one criterion of habits, namely resistance to devaluation, due to the nature of the task.' The reviewer noted this limitation prevents firm conclusions about whether sequences are habits versus goal-directed skills, though acknowledged 'overtraining was almost certainly established, and automaticity was demonstrated.'

results.result: The authors propose that attributing higher intrinsic value to familiar actions may be a mechanism for compulsions, and suggest smartphone app training has potential as a habit reversal therapeutic tool through habit replacement or distraction.
results.evaluation: The reviewer stated that 'The results are supportive of the author's conclusions' and noted the article 'is likely to be impactful.' The editor emphasized the study's 'important implications for our understanding of goal-directed versus habit learning in obsessive-compulsive disorder,' accepting these theoretical interpretations and therapeutic implications.

results.result: The current findings do not support differences between OCD and healthy individuals in sensitivity to negative score changes, unlike previous work showing increased response switching after negative feedback in OCD.
results.evaluation: Reviewers did not challenge this null finding. The reviewer's acknowledgment that results were 'not supported' for some hypotheses indicates acceptance of both positive and negative findings, and this result is consistent with the overall pattern of comparable reward sensitivity between groups.
